orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Capasso fell on the tiled basement floor of defendants’ home on June 27, 2007. She initially signed a statement saying she did not know the cause. In a later affidavit she suggested water as a possible cause.

legal_issues.finding: Capasso’s signed statement did not identify a cause. The court found her later suggestion of water insufficient to raise a genuine factual dispute, and her husband’s affidavit did not establish the floor’s condition when she fell.
The later affidavit did not overcome the earlier signed statement, and the prospect of helpful discovery did not justify postponing summary judgment under CPLR 3212(f).

evidence_discussed.description: The court considered Capasso’s signed statement and later affidavit about possible water.
The husband’s affidavit did not establish the condition of the floor at the relevant time.

quality.notes: The court treated the claim as a slip-and-fall action. Water is a proposed hazard only; no cause was established.

evidence.quote: the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Spinner, J.), entered March 24, 2010, which granted the defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
On June 27, 2007, at approximately 10:30 a.m., the plaintiff was walking on the tile floor in the basement of the defendants’ home when she fell.

In a slip-and-fall case, a plaintiffs inability to identify the cause of the fall is fatal to the action because a finding that the defendant’s negligence, if any, proximately caused the plaintiffs injuries would be based on speculation
by submitting the signed statement of the plaintiff, in which she admitted that she did not know what caused her to fall on the date of the accident

The plaintiffs affidavit, in which she identified the cause of her fall as possibly water in the area where she fell, presented a feigned issue of fact, designed to avoid the consequences of her earlier signed statement, and thus was insufficient to defeat the defendants’ motion

The Supreme Court correctly determined that the affidavit of the plaintiffs husband, also submitted in opposition to the defendants’ motion, was not probative of the condition on the floor at the time of the subject accident

The plaintiff’s contention that summary judgment was granted prematurely under the facts of this case is without merit. The belief that additional discovery might reveal something helpful to her case does not provide a basis pursuant to CPLR 3212 (f) for postponing a determination of summary judgment in this case

orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint because the trial court found the cause unidentified.

facts.factual_summary: Devoe testified that she tripped on a door saddle at the store entrance and was then struck by the sliding door. The store was described as owned, operated or maintained by defendants.

legal_issues.finding: The court applied the duty to keep premises reasonably safe and held that defendants had shown the threshold and door were free from any dangerous defect.
Devoe identified the door saddle and the sliding door in her deposition. Defendants did not establish that she was unable to identify what caused her fall.
Defendants’ expert showed neither component was dangerous or defective. The plaintiff’s expert relied on standards that did not apply to this entryway.

evidence_discussed.description: Devoe’s deposition identified the trip and subsequent contact with the door.
The defense expert’s affidavit supported the no-defect showing. The plaintiff’s expert relied on inapplicable industry standards.

quality.notes: The trip preceded the door strike. The appellate ground was absence of a dangerous defect; it rejected the trial court’s causation rationale.

evidence.quote: the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Mark I. Partnow, J.), dated September 1, 2021. The order granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries she allegedly sustained when she tripped and was struck by a sliding door in the entryway of a store owned, operated, or maintained by the defendants.
The Supreme Court granted the defendants' motion on the ground that the plaintiff did not know what had caused her to fall.
We affirm, but on a different ground.
An owner or tenant in possession of real property owes a duty to maintain the property in a reasonably safe condition
the defendants failed to establish, prima facie, that the plaintiff did not know what had caused her to fall
The plaintiff testified at her deposition that she fell because she tripped on a door saddle and the sliding door struck her.
Nevertheless, the defendants demonstrated, prima facie, through the affidavit of their expert, that neither the door saddle nor the sliding door were in a dangerous or defective condition
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact, as the industry standards relied upon by the plaintiff's expert were inapplicable to the entryway of the store.
Accordingly, we affirm the order appealed from.

orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Nelson allegedly tripped over a single riser while leaving defendants’ restaurant. The orange tile contrasted with the black rug below it. She had crossed the same step on entering about two hours earlier.

legal_issues.finding: The owners owed no duty to warn or protect against this riser once they showed it was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous.
The owners established that the single-step riser was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous. Nelson did not raise a triable issue in response.

evidence_discussed.description: Nelson testified that she was looking forward just before the accident.

quality.notes: The court granted dismissal on the owners’ motion. It did not assign comparative fault based on the plaintiff’s direction of gaze.

evidence.quote: the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Nahman, J.), entered July 12, 2011, which denied their motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.
The plaintiff allegedly tripped and fell over a single-step riser while leaving a restaurant owned by the defendants.

The step was made of orange-colored tile and stood in contrast to the black rug located on the floor below the step. The plaintiff had traversed the step, without incident, approximately two hours earlier, when she first entered the restaurant.
The plaintiff testified at her deposition that, just prior to the accident, she was looking “forward.”
a landowner has no duty to protect or warn against an open and obvious condition that is not inherently dangerous
Here, the defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by presenting evidence that the single-step riser was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to submit evidence sufficient to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.trial_court_action: Denied Tops Markets’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Wrobel alleged that she slipped on snow or ice in Tops Markets’ parking lot. She testified that it was not snowing at the time of the fall.

legal_issues.finding: Tops’s initial failure meant Wrobel did not bear the burden of showing actual notice of a preexisting condition.
The court likewise did not require Wrobel to show constructive notice of a preexisting condition.
Tops failed to establish that the injuries resulted from an ongoing storm. Wrobel testified it was not snowing, and the meteorologist’s opinion lacked record support.
The defense did not connect the injury to an ongoing storm, so Wrobel did not need to establish that an earlier condition caused the fall.
The court deemed the defense meteorologist’s opinions conclusory and unsupported.
The burden never shifted. The court denied the motion without considering the sufficiency of Wrobel’s opposition.

evidence_discussed.description: Tops submitted Wrobel’s deposition about conditions at the time of the accident.
The defense meteorologist’s opinions lacked evidentiary support.

quality.notes: The ruling concerns Tops’s failure to establish its storm defense. The court made no finding that the owner actually knew of the accumulation.

evidence.quote: Jessica Wrobel, Respondent, v Tops Markets, LLC, Appellant.

Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Erie County (Catherine R. Nugent Panepinto, J.), entered September 26, 2016. The order denied the motion of defendant for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.
Plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for injuries that she allegedly sustained when she slipped and fell on snow or ice in defendant's parking lot.
Supreme Court properly denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint
defendant failed to meet its burden of establishing that plaintiff's injuries were caused by a storm in progress
In support of its motion, defendant submitted the deposition testimony of plaintiff, who testified that it was not snowing at the time of the accident.
Moreover, the opinions of defendant's expert meteorologist are at best conclusory and have "no evidentiary support in the record"

Inasmuch as defendant failed to meet its initial burden, the burden never shifted to plaintiff "to raise a triable issue of fact 'whether the accident was caused by a slippery condition at the location where the plaintiff fell that existed prior to the storm, as opposed to precipitation from the storm in progress, and that the defendant had actual or constructive notice of the preexisting condition' "
Thus, the court properly denied defendant's motion without regard to the sufficiency of plaintiff's opposing papers

orders.trial_court_action: Granted the restaurant operator’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Cietek was a patron at defendant’s restaurant. After leaving the restroom on October 26, 2006, she slipped on a small puddle while walking toward the dining area.

legal_issues.finding: The operator met its initial burden of showing reasonably safe maintenance and absence of creation or notice.
The expert’s slippery-floor opinion identified no applicable standard and did not raise a triable issue of creation.
The assistant manager observed no water and received no complaints. Cietek raised no genuine dispute on actual notice.
The manager had been stationed about five feet away for three hours and did not see water or any other fall. Cietek did not raise a triable question of constructive notice.
The court found the cited OSHA standard inapplicable because it protected employees and Cietek was a restaurant patron.
The plaintiff’s expert found a low coefficient of friction but relied on an employee-safety standard inapplicable to a patron and cited no relevant alternative.

evidence_discussed.description: The assistant manager’s affidavit and deposition described the floor-check policy and his personal observations near the accident site.
The plaintiff’s expert submitted an affidavit addressing floor friction, but the cited standard did not apply.

quality.notes: The employee-only standard could not establish a violation as to this restaurant patron. The court separately addressed notice and creation.

evidence.quote: Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court (Platkin, J.), entered May 29, 2009 in Albany County, which granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

On October 26, 2006, plaintiff was injured in a slip and fall accident while a patron at a restaurant operated by defendant. *1629 Plaintiff had exited the restaurant’s restroom and was walking towards the dining area when she slipped on a small puddle of water and fell.
Supreme Court granted the motion and plaintiff now appeals.
We affirm.
maintained the premises in a reasonably safe condition and neither created nor had actual or constructive notice of the allegedly dangerous condition”

Here, defendant met its initial burden by providing the affidavit and deposition testimony of the assistant manager on duty the day of the accident, which established that it was defendant’s policy that all employees regularly checked the floors for spills, discarded dishes and trash.

His sworn statements also established that, although he was stationed approximately five feet from the area where plaintiff fell for three hours prior to the accident, he did not observe any water on the floor that day, nor did he receive any complaints concerning water on the floor or witness anyone else slip or fall in that area.
In opposition, plaintiff did not present any evidence raising a genuine issue of fact as to actual or constructive notice.

Regarding defendant creating a dangerous condition, plaintiff proffered the affidavit of an expert who determined that the friction coefficient of the restaurant floor did not meet industry standards and concluded that the floor was unacceptably slippery wet or dry.
a cause of action for negligence cannot be maintained against a building owner solely on the basis of an inherently slippery floor

plaintiffs expert referenced an Occupational Safety and Health Administration standard, which is inapplicable as that agency’s regula *1630 tions are limited to the safety of employees (see Kocurek v Home Depot, U.S.A.P., 286 AD2d 577, 580 [2001]), and failed to reference any other relevant standard, the expert affidavit failed to raise a triable issue of fact regarding defendant creating a dangerous condition
Accordingly, summary judgment was properly granted in defendant’s favor.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
